entry.title: fix(tests): the place canary is failed by a store the browser threw away
entry.content:
fix(tests): the place canary is failed by a store the browser threw away

targum-internal#204. `test_a_reader_opened_from_disk_keeps_what_it_was_told`
failed four times on CI since the seek fix landed, and not for either reason
this issue assumed.

Crossed in the test's own shape — one context, one page, two gotos, one
variable at a time. A lost `localStorage` write passes. A recovery delayed to
1.5s, three times `durable.js`'s 500ms patience, passes. Both together pass,
`here: True`, gap 0. So the blind start is not it, and `durable.js` does the
job it was written for.

What reproduces the transcript exactly — `words: 280`, `here: False`,
`kept: {}`, the same 3271px — is the second load on a fresh storage partition,
and nothing else does. The browser discarded this `file://` origin's storage
between the navigations, both copies, so recovery had nothing to recover and
the reader was being failed for something it cannot see. Same Chromium build
here as on the runner, so not a version difference.

The canary now asks the shelf, after the navigation, whether the place
survived it — the existing check ran in the previous document and cannot
answer for this one. Storage gone: skip, naming the cause. Storage intact and
the reader did not restore: fail, as before.

Teeth verified rather than assumed, since a test that can only pass or skip is
worthless: with `resume()` neutered in the built file and storage untouched it
fails, gap 3271, precondition true.

entry.title: fix(annotate): an absent shelf is not a current one
entry.content:
fix(annotate): an absent shelf is not a current one

`survey` on a path that does not exist returned an empty `Shelf`, which prints
"0 of 0 behind" — the reassuring version of exactly the silence this check was
written to break. A mistyped path, or a user who cannot see /var/lib/targum,
would have answered "is the box behind?" with "no".

It raises now. `preflight.check_shelf` already tested the path itself before
calling, so the deploy path still says "nothing built at <path> yet" on a first
deploy and is unchanged.

entry.title: fix(annotate): the artifact says what the lookup covered, and the box…
entry.content:
fix(annotate): the artifact says what the lookup covered, and the box says what is behind

Three cards from the annotator-staleness family, all additive: no annotator name
changes, so no cache is invalidated and nothing is re-annotated.

targum-internal#180 — `ScriptureLemmatizer.name` is fixed at wrap time, and wrapping
is not running: `lemmas()` falls through per verse. So the `p4` copy of Genesis, 0
`PART` across 20,858 tokens and read entirely by the model, carries a name identical
to the `library/` copy that carries 1,958, while the two disagree by five points of
difficulty. `Annotation.scripture_share` records what the tagging actually answered;
`0.0` (wrapped, matched nothing) is a different fact from `None` (nothing asked). A
share and not a flag, because a chapter heading never lines up. Deliberately not in
the name: a key that moved with the outcome would re-annotate a text whenever a verse
happened to align differently, and an unstable key is worse than an ambiguous one.
`measure_difficulty.by_scripture_path` reads the field and keeps the `PART` sniff only
for artifacts older than it.

targum-internal#207 — the binyan is pinned through the whole `Annotator` rather than
through `ScriptureLemmatizer`. The lemmatizer-level test was green throughout, which
is why it caught nothing while the shelf carried a binyan on 0.68% of its scripture
verbs and the same code produced ~100%. Banding, the register and the dictionary stage
run between the two. `UPOS=` is asserted beside it, the second casualty in the same
artifacts.

targum-internal#208 — `targum preflight` prints how many built texts are behind, on
every deploy and right before the `rebuild --words` that closes the gap. Three fixes
were merged, closed and believed shipped on 2026-09-03 and reached no built page;
nothing was done wrong, there was simply no line that printed "411 of 418 behind". A
warning and not a failure. The comparison moves to `annotate/versions.py` so there is
one of it, and `scripts/shelf_versions.py` imports it and keeps the detail — `--list`,
by home, and the ingester's separate question.

entry.title: feat(vocalize): DICTA's menaked points modern Hebrew, gated by register
entry.content:
feat(vocalize): DICTA's menaked points modern Hebrew, gated by register

The measurement in the two commits before this one held on both held-out
sets, so this is step 4 of targum-internal#148: the swap, and nothing that
the measurement did not earn.

`vocalize/dicta.py` wraps dictabert-large-char-menaked behind the existing
Vocalizer protocol. It loads the model's own tokenizer.json rather than what
AutoTokenizer builds under transformers 5, and assembles the marks by walking
the input rather than the tokens, so every character comes back exactly once
and a letter the model calls a mater is kept bare. Both are the bugs the
measurement found in the card's own code, and both are pinned by test. Every
output still goes through the skeleton check in base.py, as Nakdimon's does.

`vocalize.for_source` is the gate. Scripture and the pinned editions reach no
model, as before. The biblical, rabbinic and medieval shelves stay on
Nakdimon — the card says the model is not for them. The revival and modern
shelves and every upload go to the menaked; the Ben-Yehuda measurement was of
revival Hebrew and the menaked won on it. The register is read off the
catalogue, and a text the catalogue does not know is read as today's Hebrew.

The weights are 1.2 GB and never fetched inside a build: `targum models
fetch menaked` brings them, `fetch he` brings them with the annotator's, and
a machine without them points with Nakdimon and says so once. The name
`dicta/menaked/1` is the cache key, and the pipeline now reuses a stored
pointing only when its vocalizer is the one that would run, so a text
Nakdimon pointed is pointed again on its next build or `rebuild --words`,
which re-points before it re-annotates because the readings are worked out
from the pointing. SCHEMA_VERSION is untouched. The reader credits DICTA for
the vowels where the menaked made them, keyed like the annotator's credit;
LICENSING.md records the licence, the measurement and the gate.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(evals): a second held-out set for the pointing measurement, from…
entry.content:
feat(evals): a second held-out set for the pointing measurement, from Ben-Yehuda

The first corpus is DICTA's own test set, so the gap it showed could have been
house style. This adds `--corpus ben-yehuda`: 26 pointed works by 12 authors
from Project Ben-Yehuda's public domain dump, prose and poetry, none of them
among the nine Ben-Yehuda authors Nakdimon's training set names. Paragraphs
that are fully pointed are joined into lines of twenty words or more, at most
thirty lines a work, so no one novel outweighs the poets.

The gap holds on 250 lines, 5,454 words: the menaked is 0.9056 to 0.8933 on
vowels per letter (0.9102 to 0.8933 with qamats qatan folded, since these
editions never write it and the menaked does), 0.7004 to 0.6766 on exact
words, and keeps the skeleton on every line. Both models fall by seven to
seventeen points from Wikipedia to the Hebrew of 1880-1940.

Two scoring changes came with the corpus. A shin the reference leaves bare is
no longer scored on its dot: these editions dot only the sin, and a model that
dots the shin is not wrong. And the menaked's marks are now assembled by
walking the input rather than by the card's predict, which emits a character
once per token it became — the tokenizer NFKC-expands an ellipsis into three
dots, and 24 of 250 lines came back with `………` and failed the skeleton check.
The walk is versioned `/walk` in the ledger so its rows never pass for the
card's, and on the DICTA corpus it reproduces the card's numbers exactly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(store): the correction store, door 1 — every hand on a gloss is …
entry.content:
feat(store): the correction store, door 1 — every hand on a gloss is written down

The one thing no model lab has is a record of human judgement about
Hebrew at the word level, with provenance, and until now every such
judgement was thrown away the moment it was applied: a wrong gloss was
deleted from the cache by hand, a right one grounded, and nothing said
a person decided. A `correction` table now keeps what stood, what
stands, who decided (a role, never a name), the licence the judgement
is held under, and the sentence seen. `targum correct` applies the
author's hand and keeps the row; a grounding at a reader's tap writes
one too; `targum corrections` lists them. The editor's and the reader's
doors, the harness export and the notice text are the rest of
targum-internal#164, decided 2026-09-07 to start minimal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
